GDP, Inflation and Fiscal Policy: Macroeconomics for Students

Macroeconomics looks at the economy as a whole: output, prices, jobs and government finances. This guide covers the key measures and how the government influences them, and why investors follow them.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

GDP and how it is measured

  • The expenditure method adds up spending, as above.
  • The income method adds up wages, rent, interest and profit.
  • The production method adds up the value added in each sector.

GDP = C + I + G + (X − M): consumption + investment + government spending + exports − imports. With C = 60, I = 30, G = 15, X = 20 and M = 25, GDP = 100.

In India, the National Statistics Office publishes GDP estimates each quarter.

Real and nominal GDP

Nominal GDP is measured at current prices, and real GDP at constant prices, which removes inflation.

If nominal GDP grows 11% and inflation is 4%, real growth is about 1.11 ÷ 1.04 − 1 = 6.7%.

GDP per capita divides the total by the population, and is a rough measure of average income. GDP is not a complete measure of welfare, as it misses inequality, unpaid work and the environment.

Inflation and its measures

  • Inflation: a general rise in prices over time. Demand-pull inflation comes from too much spending, and cost-push inflation from rising input costs.
  • CPI: prices that households pay, which the RBI targets.
  • WPI: prices at the wholesale level.
  • GDP deflator: the broadest price measure, covering all output.
  • Deflation, disinflation and stagflation: falling prices, slowing inflation, and high inflation with weak growth, in turn.

Fiscal policy and the Union Budget

Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxes and spending. In a slowdown, it can spend more or tax less (expansionary). When the economy is overheating, it can do the reverse (contractionary).

MeasureFormula
Revenue deficitRevenue expenditure − revenue receipts
Fiscal deficitTotal expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts)
Primary deficitFiscal deficit − interest payments

Fiscal deficit shows how much the government must borrow. Heavy borrowing can push up interest rates and crowd out private investment. India's FRBM Act sets a framework for keeping this under control.

Direct and indirect taxes

BasisDirect taxIndirect tax
Paid byThe person it is charged onCollected from the buyer by the seller
ExamplesIncome tax, corporate taxGST, customs duty
BurdenCannot be shiftedPassed on to the consumer
EffectGenerally progressiveGenerally regressive

The business cycle

Economies move through expansion, peak, contraction (a recession if severe) and recovery. Different sectors tend to do better at different stages. Defensive sectors such as FMCG and pharma hold up in slowdowns, while cyclical ones such as autos, banks and metals tend to do well in recoveries.

External accounts

  • Balance of payments: all flows of money between India and the world.
  • Current account deficit: paying out more than is earned on trade in goods and services, and on transfers such as remittances.
  • Capital account: investment and borrowing flows, including FDI and FPI.
  • Exchange rate: a weaker rupee helps exporters such as IT firms, and hurts importers of oil.

Exam and interview questions

What is the difference between GDP and GNP?

GDP measures output produced inside the country. GNP adds income earned abroad by residents and subtracts income earned here by foreigners.

What is the difference between fiscal deficit and revenue deficit?

Revenue deficit compares only day-to-day income and spending. Fiscal deficit covers all spending, including capital spending, and shows the government's total borrowing need.

What is the difference between monetary and fiscal policy?

Monetary policy is run by the RBI through interest rates and liquidity. Fiscal policy is run by the government through taxes and spending.

What is stagflation?

High inflation combined with weak growth and high unemployment, which is hard to treat because the usual cure for one worsens the other.
